planting.note: Start seed indoors 6–8 weeks before the last frost and transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun once nights stay reliably above 55°F; this vigorous indeterminate vine benefits from sturdy staking.

directions: Start seed indoors and transplant deeply into rich, well-drained soil in full sun after frost danger has passed, then stake or cage the vine early. Dester is a French heirloom beefsteak prized for its smooth, rounded, deep pink-red fruit that runs unusually free of the cracking and catfacing that plague many large heirloom slicers, often reaching a pound or more with very few seeds and a thin, tender skin. The flesh is dense, low in acid, and richly sweet, making it a favorite among heirloom growers for fresh eating despite the plant's somewhat unassuming, ordinary-looking foliage. Water evenly and mulch well through fruit set, since the smooth skin is still thin enough to split under drought-then-deluge conditions; the vigorous, disease-tolerant vine keeps setting fruit steadily through a long Gulf Coast season.

common_name: Omar's Lebanese Tomato (Middle Eastern Heirloom Pink Beefsteak)

planting.note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost and transplant into deeply worked, fertile soil in full sun; the huge, heavy fruit clusters need sturdy caging or staking from an early age.

directions: Set out transplants into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after all frost danger passes, spacing plants generously to allow air movement around the sprawling vine. Omar's Lebanese is a Middle Eastern heirloom brought into wider American circulation through the Seed Savers Exchange network, grown for enormous, smooth, pale to deep pink beefsteak fruit that regularly reaches one to two pounds with a mild, low-acid, juicy sweetness. The indeterminate vines are notably productive for such a large-fruited variety, setting fruit steadily through summer heat where many other big pink slicers slow down. Provide even moisture and consistent feeding, since fruit of this size draws heavily on the plant, and support the heaviest clusters to prevent limb breakage.

common_name: Gregori's Altai Tomato (Early Siberian Red Heirloom)

planting.note: Start indoors 6 weeks before last frost; this early, cold-set variety can go into the ground as soon as night temperatures stay reliably above 50°F, giving a jump on the Gulf Coast spring crop before summer heat shuts down fruit set.

directions: Start seed indoors and transplant into full sun once nights are reliably mild, staking the moderately vigorous indeterminate vine as it grows. Gregori's Altai is a Siberian heirloom from the Altai Mountains region prized for setting medium-large, four-inch, deep red fruit with a faint golden blush at the shoulders unusually early and even in the cool, fluctuating spring temperatures that stall most other beefsteaks. The rich, well-balanced sweet-tart flavor rivals much larger, later-maturing heirlooms, and the plant's tolerance for cool nights makes it an excellent first-wave spring tomato for Gulf Coast gardens that need to beat the arrival of intense summer heat. Keep watering even as fruit sizes up to avoid cracking on the thin, tender skin.

common_name: Genuwine Tomato (Brandywine x German Johnson Cross Beefsteak)

planting.note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost and transplant into deeply worked, fertile soil in full sun; the heavy fruit clusters need sturdy staking or caging from transplant onward.

directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after frost risk passes, and stake or cage early to support the heavy fruit load. Genuwine is a modern open-pollinated selection bred by crossing Brandywine and German Johnson to combine the rich, complex flavor of Brandywine with German Johnson's smoother skin, more regular fruit shape, and improved productivity. The large, pink-red beefsteak fruit, often exceeding a pound, has a meaty, low-seed interior and a sweet, deep flavor that heirloom-tomato fans compare favorably to Brandywine itself while avoiding some of its notoriously erratic, lower-yielding habit. Feed and water consistently through fruit set, and pick as soon as fruit colors fully to avoid splitting during Gulf Coast summer rain.

common_name: Polish Linguisa Tomato (Sausage-Shaped Polish Heirloom Paste Tomato)

planting.note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost and transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; provide staking or caging, since the indeterminate vine carries a heavy load of elongated fruit.

directions: Transplant into rich, well-drained soil in full sun after last frost, staking early to support the long fruit clusters. Polish Linguisa is a Polish heirloom paste tomato named for its distinctive elongated, curved, sausage-like fruit shape, which sets it apart from the blockier Roma and San Marzano types most gardeners know. The deep red fruit is dense and meaty with very little seed cavity or juice, cooking down quickly into a thick, richly flavored sauce or paste with minimal simmering. The vigorous indeterminate vines are heavy producers over a long season; pick fruit as it colors fully and process promptly, since the thin skin is more prone to splitting after heavy rain than dedicated modern paste hybrids.
